strengths: The paper addresses a useful EDA problem: predicting post-synthesis area and delay directly from RTL could shorten hardware-design feedback loops. Representing RTL as a control-data-flow graph is well motivated, particularly for delay prediction where connectivity matters.

StructRTL combines GIN message passing, spectral positional encodings, a Transformer, two self-supervised objectives, and cross-stage distillation in a coherent framework. The manuscript is generally clear and its figures explain the pipeline effectively.

The reported improvements are substantial and consistent across MAE, MAPE, R2, and RRSE. Without distillation, StructRTL reaches area/delay R2 values of 0.7463/0.7630, compared with 0.6353/0.6639 for the strongest listed baselines; it remains strongest after distillation.

The evaluation uses 13,200 designs, considerably more than many earlier RTL-estimation studies, and includes graph, GNN, and 6.7B–7B code-model baselines. The authors also report dataset-size and label distributions and ablate each pretraining loss.
weaknesses: The experimental protocol does not support the central state-of-the-art and generalization claims. The data are split only into training and validation sets, with no untouched test set; the paper says models are trained until convergence but does not explain model selection. Hyperparameter tuning and reporting on the same validation set can substantially bias the results.

The random 80:20 split is especially concerning because designs are collected from GitHub repositories, textbooks, VeriGen, and DeepCircuitX without repository-level splitting, provenance analysis, or deduplication. Near-duplicate modules and related variants could cross the split, allowing models to exploit project or template similarity rather than generalize to unseen designs.

Both self-supervised tasks contain potential target leakage. Node embeddings are masked only after the GNN has processed the original node types, so neighboring embeddings can already encode the masked type. Likewise, edge prediction is performed after message passing over the complete graph, including the edge being predicted. Consequently, the high reconstruction accuracies and the claimed mechanism of structure learning are difficult to interpret.

The ablations do not isolate the source of the gains. Graph-GNN lacks the Transformer and positional encoding, while the StructRTL variants retain at least one pretraining objective. A same-architecture model trained end-to-end without pretraining, as well as controls that mask nodes or edges before message passing, is necessary to distinguish self-supervision from added capacity and information leakage.

Table 2 reports knowledge-distilled results for Graph-XGBoost, although the described distillation loss aligns final-layer neural activations and no corresponding XGBoost representation or procedure is defined. More generally, the paper does not explain how distillation is adapted to each baseline, making an important comparison irreproducible.

The spectral construction is technically underspecified and potentially incorrect: L = I - D_in^{-1/2} A D_out^{-1/2} is called a symmetric normalized Laplacian despite generally being nonsymmetric for a directed graph. The paper does not address complex eigenvectors, zero-degree nodes, repeated eigenvalues, or eigenbasis instability. It also omits how full Transformer attention and eigendecomposition are made feasible for graphs with up to 19,169 nodes, despite reporting batch size 16.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The promised anonymous repository link is blank, and important details are missing, including hidden dimensions, dropout, the stratified-mask minimum m, preprocessing and synthesis commands, target units, random seeds, split identities, checkpoint selection, and handling of long RTL/token sequences. Results are single numbers without variance over seeds or statistical tests.

The evaluation covers only one synthesis/mapping flow and one 130 nm library, with no cross-library, cross-tool, repository-held-out, or out-of-distribution study. It therefore does not establish robustness across realistic deployment conditions. The claim that R2 measures relative design quality is also inaccurate; rank correlations or pairwise-ordering accuracy would be more appropriate.

Dataset reporting contains inconsistencies: Table 4 assigns Eq nodes a ratio of 8.17%, but 189,418 out of the listed 2,844,911 nodes is approximately 6.66%; 8.17% corresponds instead to the Const count. The filtering statement that random simulation with meaningful outputs ensures area and delay are well-defined is not justified.

The paper provides no substantive limitations or research-ethics discussion. Because source code was gathered from GitHub repositories and textbooks, it should document licenses, redistribution permissions, provenance, overlap with upstream datasets, and safeguards against benchmark contamination. These omissions compound the reproducibility and leakage concerns.

strengths: Significance: Fast RTL area/delay estimation is practically relevant, and using CDFGs to expose hardware structure is well motivated.
Presentation: The manuscript is generally readable, with clear framework diagrams, explicit loss definitions, dataset-size statistics, and results reported using several regression metrics.
Evidence breadth: The study uses 13,200 designs, substantially more than many earlier graph-based RTL studies, and compares against handcrafted, GNN, and Verilog-LLM baselines.
The reported improvements are sizable, and the ablations suggest that both proposed auxiliary objectives contribute empirically.
weaknesses: Soundness: Both pretraining objectives leak their targets. Node types are masked only after an eight-layer GNN has processed the complete node features, so the masked type can already be encoded in neighboring embeddings. Edge prediction likewise uses GNN features and Laplacian positional encodings computed from the complete graph, including the edges being predicted. The experiments therefore do not establish that the model learns to reconstruct genuinely hidden structure.

Soundness: Equation 2 is described as a symmetric normalized Laplacian for a directed graph, but I-D_in^{-1/2} A D_out^{-1/2} is generally non-symmetric. Its eigenvalues/eigenvectors may be complex and cannot simply be ordered as stated; zero-degree input/output nodes also make the inverse degree factors undefined. No handling of these issues is provided.

Evaluation: Results are reported on a single random 80/20 training-validation split, with no independent test set, repeated seeds, uncertainty, or statistical tests. Designs gathered from repositories and textbooks are not deduplicated or split by repository/design family, creating a serious risk that closely related modules occur on both sides of the split.

The main attribution is underdetermined. Graph-GNN lacks the Transformer used by StructRTL, while no randomly initialized supervised GIN-plus-Transformer baseline is reported. Consequently, the results do not isolate self-supervised pretraining from architecture size or capacity. Important ablations for positional encodings, post-GNN versus properly masked inputs, and pretraining data are also absent.

The knowledge-distillation comparison is insufficiently specified and internally problematic. Table 2 claims KD results for every baseline, including XGBoost, although the activation-alignment loss in Equation 9 is not applicable to XGBoost as described. Moreover, StructRTL's area MAE and MAPE worsen from 0.3649/0.06 to 0.3856/0.07 with KD, contradicting the claim that KD improves all methods.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the anonymous code/data repository field is blank. Essential details such as embedding dimensions, minimum stratified-mask count m, node ordering, batching or truncation, random seeds, exact dataset composition, synthesis scripts/tool versions, and baseline/KD implementations are missing. Applying full self-attention to graphs containing up to 19,169 nodes also raises major memory and scalability questions that are not addressed.

Metric reporting is ambiguous about whether MAE and MAPE are computed in logarithmic or original physical units. The assertion that R2 measures relative ordering is incorrect, and RRSE is redundant with R2 under the given definitions. Evaluation under only one technology library and synthesis flow further limits evidence of practical generalization.

Originality is modest: the method mainly combines standard GIN/Transformer components, GraphMAE-style node reconstruction, edge prediction, and a distillation strategy explicitly inspired by prior work. The claimed RTL-specific adaptations are precisely where the target-leakage problems arise.

Limitations and ethics: There is no substantive limitations discussion, despite scalability, distribution shift, synthesis-flow dependence, and potential leakage being central concerns. The paper also does not discuss licensing, provenance, or permitted redistribution of RTL collected from GitHub repositories. Table 4 contains apparent statistical errors as well—for example, the listed counts imply approximately 6.66% Equality nodes, not 8.17%, and the displayed percentages sum to more than 100%.

strengths: Soundness: StructRTL is a coherent combination of CDFG-based representation learning, masked-node and edge-prediction objectives, and post-mapping knowledge distillation. The reported improvements are substantial and consistent across MAE, MAPE, R2, and RRSE; with distillation, StructRTL reaches R2 values of 0.8676 for area and 0.8872 for delay, outperforming every RTL-only baseline.

Significance: Fast RTL quality estimation is practically important, and the use of 13,200 designs is meaningfully larger than many earlier graph-based RTL studies. The especially strong delay results support the intuition that explicit circuit structure can be more informative than token-only representations.

Originality: Applying graph self-supervision tailored to CDFGs and combining it with cross-stage supervision from post-mapping netlists is a useful, moderately original synthesis of existing ideas. Stratified masking and class-balanced focal loss sensibly address the extreme node-type imbalance.

Presentation: The motivation, architecture, training objectives, and main comparisons are generally easy to follow. Figures clearly communicate the representation-learning and distillation pipelines, and the appendix provides useful node-type and dataset-size statistics.

The experiments include competitive LLM-based, hand-engineered, and end-to-end GNN baselines, as well as separate removals of both pretraining losses. No direct human-subject or deployment-safety concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: The evaluation uses only a random 80:20 training/validation split and reports results on the validation set; there is no untouched test set. The manuscript does not explain whether repository families, related modules, generated variants, or near-duplicates are kept in the same partition. Leakage between closely related RTL designs could substantially inflate the reported generalization performance.

The central claim that self-supervised learning causes the gains is not adequately isolated. The closest Graph-GNN baseline lacks StructRTL's Transformer and positional encoding, while the ablations remove one pretraining objective at a time but never compare against the complete GIN-Transformer architecture trained from scratch. Differences in capacity or architecture could therefore explain part of the improvement.

The stated directed-graph Laplacian L = I - D_in^{-1/2} A D_out^{-1/2} is generally not symmetric, despite being called symmetric. Its eigenvectors can be non-orthogonal or complex, and the paper's sign-flip treatment does not resolve repeated-eigenvalue or basis ambiguities. The exact positional-encoding construction consequently requires technical clarification.

The evidence is limited to one random split, one synthesis flow, and one SkyWater 130 nm library. There are no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, statistical tests, held-out design families, cross-dataset evaluation, or transfer across technologies. Thus the state-of-the-art and generalization claims are stronger than the evidence supports.

Baseline fairness and experimental details are incomplete: parameter counts and hidden dimensions are absent, the depth and tuning of Graph-GNN are unclear, and it is not shown that baselines received comparable tuning or compute. The paper also omits important ablations for positional encoding, stratified masking, class-balanced loss, and knowledge-distillation loss components.

Reproducibility is presently weak. The appendix's anonymous repository field is blank, while details such as the minimum-per-class masking value, preprocessing and deduplication rules, precise dataset membership, random seeds, checkpoint selection, negative sampling, and whether the pretrained encoder is frozen or fine-tuned are missing.

The paper does not clearly state whether reported errors are computed in log space or after transforming predictions back to physical units. If MAPE is measured on log labels, it is not an interpretable percentage error in area or delay. Moreover, R2 does not directly measure relative design ordering, contrary to the justification given; rank correlations or optimization-selection metrics would better support that use case.

The claimed practical speed advantage is not measured. CDFG extraction, Laplacian eigendecomposition, and quadratic Transformer attention may be expensive for graphs reaching 19,169 nodes, yet no preprocessing time, inference latency, memory use, synthesis-speed comparison, or failure-rate analysis is reported.

There is no substantive limitations discussion. Dataset filtering may bias the benchmark toward readily parsable and synthesizable designs, and generalization to industrial RTL, alternative tools, or other process libraries is unexamined. The paper should also document the licenses and permitted reuse of RTL collected from GitHub repositories and textbooks.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical EDA problem: obtaining rapid area and delay feedback before full synthesis. Using CDFGs gives the model an appropriate structural inductive bias, especially for delay prediction.

The empirical scope is substantial. The authors evaluate 13,200 designs, compare against graph- and LLM-based predictors, ablate both pretraining losses and architectural components, examine limited-label settings, and add functionality- and size-shift experiments.

The reported predictive results are strong: without distillation, StructRTL reaches R² values of 0.7463 for area and 0.7630 for delay, and it retains an advantage over the reported LLM baselines under the alternative splits.
The 30M-parameter model is much smaller than the 7B-parameter LLM baselines, and the post-mapping teacher is needed only during training. This is potentially useful for deployment.

The presentation is generally clear and visually polished. The appendix usefully reports class imbalance, sequential-versus-combinational performance, memory scaling, and limitations concerning large designs, sequential circuits, and technology-node transfer.
weaknesses: The central self-supervised objectives contain substantial information leakage. Node masking occurs only after the 8-layer GIN has processed the unmasked node type, so the target type has already influenced its own representation and neighboring representations. Likewise, edge prediction uses embeddings produced by message passing over the complete graph, including the edges being predicted. These objectives therefore do not demonstrate reconstruction from genuinely hidden node or edge information, undermining the central methodological interpretation.

The evaluation does not adequately establish statistical reliability. Results appear to come from single splits and runs, with no random-seed variation, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite repeated claims of significant improvements. Several gains from the proposed objectives are relatively modest and could be sensitive to training or split variance.

Dataset independence is insufficiently controlled. Designs are pooled from datasets containing GitHub, textbook, and LLM-generated examples, but no deduplication, repository-level split, provenance breakdown, or near-clone analysis is reported. A random design-level split can place variants or duplicates across training and validation. The proposed functional split relies on text-embedding clustering with an arbitrary k=50, without validating that clusters actually correspond to disjoint functionality.

The label and metric protocol is ambiguous. Targets are logarithmically transformed, but the paper does not clearly state whether MAE and MAPE are computed in log space or after transforming predictions back to physical area and delay. If computed in log space, these quantities lack their usual engineering interpretation. Moreover, R² does not directly measure pairwise relative quality, contrary to the paper's stated motivation; rank correlation or ranking accuracy should be reported on the main test sets.

The industrial evaluation is too weak to support the practical out-of-distribution claims. It contains only 51 pairs, reports no uncertainty, gives no information about quality gaps or pair selection, and includes no competing model or simple heuristic baseline. Thus, accuracies of 82.35% and 88.23% cannot establish superiority or robust industrial generalization.

The scalability claim is incomplete. Full Transformer attention and Laplacian eigendecomposition are costly, memory reaches 52.18 GB at only 20,000 nodes, and designs above 100,000 nodes are not evaluated. The reported 145x speedup apparently compares model inference with synthesis while not clearly accounting for Yosys conversion, CDFG extraction, positional-encoding eigendecomposition, or preprocessing.

The positional-encoding definition is technically questionable: Equation 2 is called a symmetric normalized Laplacian, but using separate directed in- and out-degree matrices generally makes the displayed matrix nonsymmetric. The manuscript does not explain how potentially complex eigenpairs are ordered or handled.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The sentence claiming open-source code has no URL, and the paper omits exact data manifests and splits, deduplication procedures, random seeds, key implementation dimensions, synthesis scripts and tool configurations, precise library version, and sufficient runtime-measurement details.

Originality is moderate rather than high: the architecture combines standard GIN, Transformer, Laplacian positional encodings, masked reconstruction, link prediction, and a previously proposed cross-stage distillation idea. The RTL-specific integration is useful, but the paper overstates novelty, especially given the leakage issue.
The impact statement is boilerplate. Licensing and redistribution conditions for aggregated GitHub designs and confidentiality or release status of the industrial modules are not discussed.

strengths: The manuscript is clearly organized and motivates an important EDA problem. CDFGs are a sensible representation for exposing control and data dependencies that token-only models may capture poorly. The reported empirical gains are sizable: without distillation, StructRTL improves validation R2 over the strongest CodeV baseline from 0.6353 to 0.7463 for area and from 0.5277 to 0.7630 for delay. It also outperforms the baselines under function- and size-based splits.

The evaluation is broader than the main tables alone: it includes objective and architectural ablations, limited-label experiments, combinational-versus-sequential results, size-shift tests, 51 industrial design pairs, and runtime/memory measurements.

The model is much smaller than the 7B-parameter LLM baselines, and the paper honestly reports limitations involving sequential circuits, technology-node transfer, large-graph memory, and preliminary partitioning.
The work appears potentially useful to the specialized RTL-quality-estimation community, especially if the evaluation and pretraining methodology are repaired.
weaknesses: Soundness: both self-supervised objectives contain serious target leakage. Masked-node prediction masks only post-GNN embeddings, after an eight-layer GIN has processed the unmasked node types; the target node's type can therefore propagate into neighboring embeddings before masking. Likewise, edge prediction uses embeddings computed by a GNN on the complete graph without removing the predicted edges, as well as Laplacian encodings computed from that graph. High pretraining accuracies can consequently arise from recovering information already exposed to the encoder. This undermines the central claim that the objectives learn nontrivial transferable structural knowledge.

Soundness: the stated directed-graph Laplacian, I-D_in^{-1/2}((A+A^T)/2)D_out^{-1/2}, is generally not symmetric when in- and out-degrees differ, despite being called a symmetric normalized Laplacian. Its eigenvalues may not be real and ordering the 'smallest' eigenvalues is not well defined as written. The implementation and handling of disconnected or zero-degree nodes are not specified.

Evaluation validity: the primary result uses only a random 80/20 train-validation split over designs pooled from overlapping public, textbook, GitHub, and LLM-generated sources. No deduplication, repository-level grouping, or held-out test set is described, leaving substantial risk of template, variant, or repository leakage. The later text-embedding/k-means split does not establish functional disjointness and itself depends on an opaque external embedding service.

The paper reports single point estimates with no repeated splits, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, yet repeatedly calls small differences 'significant.' Hyperparameter choice and training to 'full convergence' on the same validation set further make the reported validation results vulnerable to selection bias.

Metric interpretation is problematic. The labels are log-transformed, and values in the tables appear to be evaluated in log space, but the paper presents MAE and MAPE as though they measured physical area and delay. MAPE on logarithms lacks the usual percentage-error interpretation. The claim that R2 measures the relative quality or ordering of two designs is also incorrect; ranking should be evaluated with pairwise accuracy, Spearman correlation, or Kendall tau. RRSE is redundant because its stated definition makes it exactly sqrt(1-R2).

The experiments do not cleanly isolate the proposed self-supervision. Graph-GNN changes both architecture and training, while the two objective ablations each retain the other objective. A fully supervised GIN-plus-Transformer baseline with identical architecture, capacity, optimization budget, and no pretraining is needed. Strong graph-transformer and standard GraphMAE/MaskGAE baselines are also absent, weakening the originality and causal claims.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The introduction says the code is open-sourced but provides no URL. The paper omits exact dataset membership and deduplication, train/validation indices, synthesis and ABC scripts, liberty-file corner, timing constraints, top-module selection, preprocessing time, seed information, and several architectural dimensions. The industrial designs are unavailable.

The claimed 145x speedup compares model inference with synthesis, but it is not stated whether Yosys compilation, RTLIL parsing, CDFG construction, Laplacian eigendecomposition, and data transfer are included. Excluding these stages makes the comparison misleading. Moreover, inference reaches 52.18 GB at 20,000 nodes, while the proposed partitioning workaround is only a small pilot and slightly harms area ranking.

Originality is limited: the method combines a conventional GIN, Transformer, Laplacian positional encodings, masked-node and edge reconstruction objectives, and a distillation strategy explicitly inspired by prior work. The domain-specific integration may be useful, but the paper currently overstates methodological novelty.

The dataset-quality and ethics discussion is superficial. Random simulation with 'meaningful outputs' does not establish functional correctness, and the manuscript does not discuss licenses, provenance, duplication, security-sensitive hardware, or confidentiality procedures for the industrial designs. These are not necessarily fatal ethical problems, but they require documentation.

Overall, the promising empirical pattern does not compensate for leakage inside the central pretraining objectives and an evaluation protocol that cannot yet establish leakage-free generalization. These are substantial rather than cosmetic revisions, supporting a Reject rating.

strengths: Significance: Fast RTL quality estimation is a useful EDA problem, and the reported 145× inference-versus-synthesis speedup suggests practical value, although preprocessing time is not included.

Soundness: Across the authors' dataset, StructRTL consistently improves over graph-feature, end-to-end GNN, and frozen CodeV baselines. Without distillation, it reaches R² values of 0.7463 for area and 0.7630 for delay, versus 0.6353 and 0.6639 for the strongest respective baselines.

The evaluation is broader than usual: it includes component and architectural ablations, limited-label experiments, function- and size-shifted splits, combinational versus sequential analysis, scalability measurements, and 102 industrial modules.

Originality: Combining an explicit CDFG representation with post-GNN masking, edge prediction, and cross-stage netlist distillation is a coherent, domain-informed formulation. The individual ingredients are established, but their integration for RTL quality estimation provides a useful contribution.

Presentation is generally clear and well organized. The figures explain the pipeline effectively, and the appendix discusses computational scaling, sequential-circuit performance, technology-node transfer, and other limitations honestly.
No major research-ethics concern is apparent; the work could reduce synthesis compute. The limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges scaling, sequential designs, and technology dependence.
weaknesses: The main soundness concern is evaluation leakage and model selection. The headline results use only a random 80:20 train/validation split assembled from overlapping GitHub-, textbook-, and LLM-derived sources, with no duplicate/design-family analysis and no untouched test set. Near-duplicate modules or variants can therefore cross the split. The embedding-plus-k-means functional split is helpful but does not establish repository-, generator-, or design-family-level independence.

All reported results appear to be single runs, without confidence intervals, statistical tests, or variation across data splits. Consequently, repeated claims of 'significant' improvement are unsupported statistically, especially for the 51-pair industrial evaluation.

The positional-encoding mathematics is internally inconsistent. Equation 2 calls its construction a symmetric normalized Laplacian, but D_in^{-1/2}((A+A^T)/2)D_out^{-1/2} is generally not symmetric when in- and out-degrees differ. Its eigenvalues need not have the assumed real ordering, making selection of the 'smallest' eigenvectors underspecified. This is central to the architecture and must be corrected or reconciled with the implementation.

The industrial result does not include any baseline, uncertainty estimate, or information about how the private designs were selected relative to training data. Thus 82.35%/88.23% pairwise accuracy alone does not substantiate the claimed out-of-distribution superiority or practical generalization.

The paper says R² measures relative design quality, but R² measures explained variance rather than ranking quality. Rank correlation or pairwise accuracy should be reported on the public evaluation as well. It is also unclear whether MAE/RRSE are computed in log space or after inverse transformation, limiting interpretation of absolute accuracy.

Originality is moderate for ICML: GIN-plus-Transformer modeling, masked-node prediction, edge prediction, Laplacian encodings, and feature-level distillation are established techniques. The adaptation is sensible, but comparison to stronger modern graph self-supervised/graph-transformer alternatives is missing, so the source of the gains is not fully isolated.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the submitted manuscript: the sentence 'The code is open-sourced at' has no URL; the exact dataset, deduplication procedure, fixed splits, seeds, hidden dimensions, and several implementation details are unavailable. Algorithm 1 also does not actually guarantee at least m masked nodes per class because it may resample nodes already masked.

The claimed latency advantage compares model inference alone against synthesis, apparently excluding Yosys/RTLIL parsing, CDFG extraction, and Laplacian eigendecomposition. Memory reaches 52.18 GB at only 20,000 nodes, and the partitioning study is preliminary, which materially limits deployment on large industrial designs.

The impact statement is boilerplate. Dataset provenance, licensing, handling of repository code, and risks from inaccurate quality predictions in hardware-design workflows deserve explicit treatment. Overall, the promising results merit consideration, but these evidential and reproducibility gaps prevent the work from yet being a technically reliable ICML acceptance.
